name: Ryan Kavanagh
presenting_complaint: Sudden generalised rash, throat tightness and wheeze after eating at a cafe

medical_history.social: Works as a graphic designer. Non-smoker. Occasional alcohol. Lives with partner.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 27-year-old man is brought to ED by ambulance 20 minutes after eating a satay dish at a cafe. He has widespread urticaria, facial and lip swelling, audible wheeze, a feeling of throat tightness and light-headedness. Obs: BP 82/48, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 89% on room air, GCS 15. He has a known peanut allergy and mild asthma.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Timing of onset relative to exposure (symptoms within ~20 min of eating satay/peanut-containing food)
Known peanut allergy and previous reaction severity
Airway/breathing symptoms: throat tightness, difficulty swallowing, change in voice, wheeze, shortness of breath
Circulatory/CNS symptoms: light-headedness, feeling faint, sense of impending doom
Skin symptoms: generalised hives, itch, lip/facial swelling
Asthma history and current inhaler use; ask about beta-blocker/ACE-inhibitor use
Prior anaphylaxis episodes and whether patient carries an adrenaline autoinjector
objective: Primary survey A-E with continuous monitoring (SpO2, ECG, NIBP)
Airway assessment for stridor, tongue/lip/oropharyngeal swelling, hoarse voice
Respiratory exam: bilateral wheeze, increased work of breathing, RR 30, SpO2 89%
Circulatory exam: hypotension BP 82/48, tachycardia HR 128, prolonged cap refill
Skin: widespread urticaria and angioedema documented
Recognise this meets criteria for anaphylaxis (skin plus airway/breathing plus circulatory involvement)
assessment: Primary diagnosis: Anaphylaxis (likely peanut trigger) with respiratory and cardiovascular compromise
Document severity: hypotensive and hypoxic = severe/life-threatening anaphylaxis
Consider and exclude differentials: acute severe asthma, vasovagal syncope, scombroid/food reaction, panic attack — but treat as anaphylaxis given multisystem features
plan: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh IMMEDIATELY; repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement
Lay patient flat (supine) with legs elevated; do NOT sit or stand the patient up
Remove/stop the trigger; call for help (MET/ED consultant)
High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather to target SpO2 greater than 94%; insert large-bore IV access
IV fluid bolus normal saline 20 mL/kg (approx 1000-2000 mL) for hypotension, repeat as needed
If refractory/persistent hypotension: commence adrenaline infusion and escalate to ICU
Serum tryptase (ideally within 1-2 h), monitor for biphasic reaction with minimum 4-6 h observation
On recovery: document allergy prominently, prescribe adrenaline autoinjector, provide ASCIA action plan, refer to immunology/allergy, incident report if drug-related

critical_errors: Leading with antihistamine or corticosteroid instead of IM adrenaline — they do NOT treat anaphylaxis and delay the life-saving drug
Sitting or standing the patient up (or leaving them sitting up) instead of lying flat with legs raised — can precipitate cardiac arrest from an empty ventricle
Giving adrenaline as an IV bolus first-line in a patient with a pulse instead of IM adrenaline (IV bolus risks arrhythmia/ischaemia)
Delaying adrenaline while awaiting IV access, bloods or senior review
must_not_miss: Anaphylaxis recognised and treated with IM adrenaline as the first action
Airway compromise (stridor/angioedema) anticipated with early call for airway/anaesthetic help
Biphasic reaction anticipated with an adequate observation period before discharge
